sessionTitle: GitHub Agentic Workflows: Automation That Actually Reads the Room

announcements.name: GitHub Agentic Workflows enters public preview
announcements.shortDescription: The capability ships in public preview the week after the session, with a companion website and ecosystem of existing workflow templates.
announcements.longDescription: GitHub Agentic Workflows is being released in public preview the week after the session, letting developers automate CI/CD, triage test failures, create issues, generate daily repo reports, and open pull requests. There is a companion website that is part of the offering, along with a deep ecosystem of existing agentic workflow types. The session also includes a GitHub Skills exercise attendees can run with their own GitHub handle to learn the capability firsthand.

announcements.name: Markdown-defined workflows replace hand-written YAML
announcements.shortDescription: Workflows are authored as Markdown files (optionally generated with Copilot) and compiled into a YAML "lock file" that GitHub Actions runs.
announcements.longDescription: Instead of having to know YAML for GitHub Actions, developers can define their workflows in Markdown, and can even use Copilot to create those Markdown files, which are then compiled into an agentic workflow. This addresses how traditional automation and CI is rigid and prone to syntax errors that are hard to identify. The agentic approach makes it easier to automate CI/CD, triage test failures, create issues, produce daily reports, and open pull requests.

announcements.name: Model-agnostic agent backing
announcements.shortDescription: Workflows can run on Copilot, Claude [inferred], Codex, or Gemini to diagnose test failures, open pull requests, and recommend stack updates.
announcements.longDescription: The agentic workflows are backed by agents and models, supporting Copilot, Claude [inferred], Codex [inferred] ("clawed codecs"), or Gemini—any of the models. These can dynamically diagnose test failures, open pull requests to make changes, update your stack, and give recommendations. There is already a deep ecosystem available for different types of agentic workflows.

announcements.name: "Safe outputs" security model
announcements.shortDescription: The agent receives only read access to the repository; a separate post-run workflow step holds the permissions to create issues or pull requests, segregating responsibilities.
announcements.longDescription: For agentic workflows to be secure, the agent is not given any permissions besides read access to the repository. Instead, a mechanism called "safe output" runs after the agent completes, and that workflow step holds the access to perform actions such as creating an issue or a pull request, segregating those responsibilities from the agent. This ensures the agent cannot hallucinate, delete the code base, or remove files, keeping the developer in control of what gets merged or discarded.

announcements.name: Hands-on GitHub Skills exercise
announcements.shortDescription: An accompanying Skills exercise built around a fictitious "Mona" website lets attendees reproduce the demo using their own GitHub handle.
announcements.longDescription: An accompanying GitHub Skills exercise lets attendees use their own GitHub handle to learn how agentic workflows work firsthand. The exercise centers on a fictitious Mona website tasked with looking at GitHub updates through blogs, change logs, and repository notes, then constantly generating updates that produce a pull request which can be merged directly or peer reviewed. Walking through the exercise in an issue, GitHub Agentic Workflows can automatically install itself and create a PR showing how to install it in the repository.
